A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original question-classification and reconstruction experiments on OneStop, including Table 1, Figure 3, and appendix results.

after.justification: v2 reports original selection and reconstruction experiments, including updated results and additional prompt/input comparisons in Tables 11 and 13.

M1.justification: DalEye-Llama changes from the fixation triples and prompt in v1 Appendix E.6 to a paragraph-plus-scanpath prompt with next-saccade direction in v2 Appendix B.2. Word-level and combined representations are also introduced. These are limited input adaptations within the retained Llama/LoRA approach.

E1.justification: Both use the OneStop information-seeking subset: 180 native English readers and 486 questions over 162 paragraphs. Selection/classification, reconstruction, and generalization to new participants, texts, and both remain unchanged. The added representation experiments retain this coverage; New Item and New Text denote the same regime.

E2.justification: Corresponding selection comparisons retain chance, both reading-time similarity baselines, Haller RNN, RoBERTEye-Fixations, DalEye-LLaVA, and DalEye-Llama. Reconstruction retains both incorrect-human-question baselines, GPT-4o, and text-only Llama 3.1. The latter already existed under the arbitrary-question terminology; new DalEye-Llama configurations are within-model ablations.

E3.justification: v2 adds evaluation of all combinations of two prompts and three DalEye-Llama input representations. The existing article-level ten-fold splits, 64/17/19% training/validation/test allocation, training budgets, model sizes, and five reconstruction metrics remain unchanged in the reported protocols.

E4.justification: v2 Tables 11 and 13 add systematic prompt and representation sensitivity analyses for selection and reconstruction, absent from v1. They test whether fixation-level, word-level, or combined inputs work best under two prompts, showing substantial weaknesses of the word-level alternatives. The generation example and question-categorizer validation are retained.

E5.justification: Both report 95% confidence intervals, reconstruction bootstrapping with n=1000, and the same mixed-effects comparisons with participant and paragraph random intercepts and slopes. No new seed counts, repeated-run disclosures, or uncertainty estimation procedures are reported. Changed interval widths and significance outcomes are result changes.

E6.justification: DalEye-Llama's aggregate selection accuracies change from 38.1/60.3/50.9% to 39.2/61.4/52.5% across All/Different/Same Spans (v1 Table 1; v2 Table 2). Reconstruction results and baseline scores are extensively revised: DalEye-Llama's New Item QA accuracy changes from 53.9% to 65.1% (Tables 9 and 12). Tables 11 and 13 add variant results. DalEye-Llama's inputs changed, so these numbers do not establish gains under identical settings.

T1.justification: The task mappings, reading-time-weighted embedding and cosine-similarity definitions, and RoBERTEye fixation-fusion equations remain mathematically equivalent after notation changes. The chance-probability enumeration in v1 Appendix B is retained in v2 Table 1. No new theoretical results or proofs appear.

C1.justification: Both present arbitrary, text-specific reading-goal decoding as a new challenge, formulate selection/classification and reconstruction tasks, and introduce discriminative and generative eye/text modeling approaches. The principal conclusion remains successful selection with promising but challenging reconstruction. Revised abstract wording and emphasis on existing baselines and applications do not materially change this scope.

C2.justification: v1 Section 9's detailed limitations concerning paragraph length, STARC question requirements, news-domain coverage, native-English sampling, laboratory reading, and transfer to lower-quality eye trackers are removed. v2 retains broader ethical cautions and calls for additional data, but omits these specific qualifications. It also adds interpretation of input sensitivity and expands the application discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds explicit Haller RNN features, extensive eye-movement and word-feature definitions in Table 3, new input templates, an Unsloth version, and direct dataset access instructions. Most hyperparameters and hardware disclosures remain unchanged. Conversely, v1's exact DalEye-LLaVA conversation template, complete Llama scanpath example, 1000 Hz sampling disclosure, and Julia MixedModels attribution are omitted.

R1.justification: Section 7 drops the broad multimodal-LLM strand covering vision, time series, EEG, and ECG, and expands positioning within gaze-based NLP and cognitive-state decoding. Added works include Bolliger et al. (2023), Deng et al. (2023, 2024), and López-Cardona et al. (2025). The procedural-versus-semantic task distinction remains; Shubi's 2024-to-2025 citation change is a publication update.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, model explanations, results narrative, and discussion. It renames classification to selection and item to text, incorporates baselines into the discriminative-model section, and substantially reorganizes the appendices. A reproducibility section is added and the standalone limitations section is removed.

P2.justification: The paper changes from two-column to single-column layout, with extensively redrawn and regrouped diagrams. Baseline diagrams move into main-text Figure 3, and the chance breakdown becomes Table 1. Reconstruction Figure 4 combines two generalization regimes in grouped bars; the third remains in Table 12. Feature and ablation tables are added.

improvement.justification: The new input ablations and feature definitions improve methodological transparency and support input-design choices. However, v2 removes v1's concrete generalizability limitations. Its Section 6.1 also retains the claim that Haller RNN outperforms generative models in every evaluation, although Table 2 gives Same Span accuracy of 52.1% versus DalEye-Llama's 52.5%. These benefits and losses leave the net quality direction unclear; higher scores with revised inputs alone do not resolve that tradeoff.
